title: Cantar de mio Cid
titleEn: The Song of the Cid — Martín Antolínez supplies the camp; the sand-filled chests are pawned to Raquel and Vidas (tiradas 5–9, lines 65–173)
part: Tiradas 5–9 · Martín Antolínez supplies the camp; the sand-filled chests are pawned to Raquel and Vidas (lines 65–173)
source: Ramón Menéndez Pidal (ed.), Poema de mio Cid, 2.ª edición corregida (Clásicos Castellanos 24; Madrid: Ediciones de “La Lectura”, 1923), pp. 128–136, lines 65–173 (tiradas 5–9). Text follows Pidal's critical text exactly, including its old accentuation and mixed spellings; Pidal's italics (his editorial restorations) are shown in [brackets], and a line he restores whole is flagged in its note. Line numbers are Pidal's. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed twelfth-century Castilian. Translations made fresh from the Old Spanish; Pidal's notes and vocabulary (1908–11) the lexical aids.

sentences.t:
Martín Antolínez, el Burgalés conplido,
a mio Çid e alos s[o]s abástales de pan e de vino;
sentences.l:
Martín Antolínez, the Burgalese, right accomplished,
to my Çid and to his men he-furnishes-them with bread and with wine;
sentences.i: Martín Antolínez, that accomplished man of Burgos, supplies my Çid and his men with bread and wine.
sentences.n: Tirada 5 (assonance í-o) — Martín Antolínez provisions the exiles' camp out of his own stores, and asks to ride out with them. el Burgalés = 'the man of Burgos'; conplido = 'complete, accomplished', a term of praise that comes back four lines later for the Çid himself. abástales = abasta + les, 'he supplies them', the object pronoun fused onto the verb as constantly in this poem. s[o]s = sos = sus 'his (men)', with Pidal restoring the older vowel.

sentences.t:
non lo conpra, ca él se lo avie consigo;
de todo conducho bien los ovo bastidos.
sentences.l:
not it does-he-buy, for he to-himself it had with-him;
with all provender well them he-had furnished.
sentences.i: He does not buy it: he had it by him already; with every kind of victual he furnished them well.
sentences.n: conducho = provisions, victuals (Latin conductus) — the word covers everything an army eats. se lo avie consigo: aver again as a full verb, 'he had it with him' — Martín Antolínez brings the stores out of Burgos at his own risk rather than buying under the king's ban. ovo bastidos = 'he had furnished', aver + past participle with the participle still agreeing with its object (los … bastidos); bastir 'to furnish, rig out' returns as the Çid's word for the chests at v. 85.

sentences.t:
Pagós mio Çid el Campeador [conplido]
e todos los otros que van a so çervicio.
sentences.l:
Pleased-himself my Çid the Campeador [accomplished]
and all the others who go in his service.
sentences.i: My Çid the accomplished Campeador was well content, and so were all the others who go in his service.
sentences.n: Pagós = pagóse, 'was satisfied, was pleased' — pagarse runs all through this part in both its senses, pleasure and payment (vv. 129, 141, 146). [conplido] is Pidal's restoration: the same epithet given to Martín Antolínez in v. 65. The extra verse is numbered 69b so that the traditional line-count stays undisturbed, as with 14b and 16b in the opening tiradas. so çervicio = su servicio.

sentences.t:
Fabló Martín Antolínez, odredes lo que a dicho:
“ya Canpeador, en buen ora f[o]stes naçido!
sentences.l:
Spoke Martín Antolínez, you-will-hear what he has said:
“O Campeador, in a good hour you-were born!
sentences.i: Martín Antolínez spoke — you shall hear what he said: “O Campeador, born in a good hour!
sentences.n: odredes = oiréis, 'you will hear' (oír with the old -edes ending): the minstrel turns aside to his listeners in mid-narrative. Canpeador, with n for m, as the copyist writes it. en buen ora f[o]stes naçido is the poem's honorific formula in its birth-form, 'born in a good hour'; f[o]stes = fuestes, the archaic second-person-plural preterite of ser, used respectfully to one man. The sword-form of the same formula opens the next tirada.

sentences.t:
esta noch y[a]gamos e vay[á]mosnos al matino,
ca acusado seré de lo que vos he seruido,
en ira del rey Alffons yo seré metido.
sentences.i: Let us lodge here tonight and be gone in the morning, for I shall be accused for the service I have done you, and I shall be put under King Alfonso's wrath.
sentences.n: y[a]gamos, present subjunctive of yazer 'to lie down, to spend the night' (Latin iacere), with Pidal restoring the a. vay[á]mosnos = vayámonos, the verb's -s still standing before the pronoun. en ira del rey … seré metido is a legal idiom, not a figure of speech: to be put into the king's ira is to be formally disgraced and banished — the very condition the Çid is in. Alffons = Alfonso, shortened as the copyist writes it.

sentences.i: If I come out of this with you, safe and alive, sooner or later the king will want me for a friend; and if not, I do not value at a fig whatever I leave behind.”
sentences.n: con vusco = con vos, the old fused form; it returns as convus[c]o at v. 168. querer m'a = me querrá — the split future: infinitive + pronoun + the reduced auxiliary a (from ha, 'has', 3rd person — the subject here is el rey), the same split-verb trick as the split conditional conbidar le ien in the opening tiradas, but with the future auxiliary rather than the conditional one. non … un figo: this language measures contempt in worthless small things, a fig here and a bad penny at v. 165.

sentences.t:
Fabló mio Çid, el que en buen ora çinxo espada:
“Martín Antolínez, sodes ardida lança!
sentences.l:
Spoke my Çid, he who in a good hour girded sword:
“Martín Antolínez, you-are a bold lance!
sentences.i: My Çid spoke, he who girded on his sword in a good hour: “Martín Antolínez, you are a bold lance!
sentences.n: Tirada 6 (assonance á-a) — the Çid, with the gold and silver all spent, proposes two chests filled with sand. el que en buen ora çinxo espada is the sword-form of the formula just used in its birth-form at v. 71: the two halves of the poem's praise-language stand in consecutive tiradas. çinxo is the strong preterite of çeñir (Latin cinxit). ardida lança, 'bold lance', is the weapon standing for the man who carries it.

sentences.t:
si yo bivo, doblar vos he la soldada.
Espeso e el oro e toda la plata,
bien lo ve[e]des que yo no trayo [nada],
sentences.l:
if I live, to-double to-you I-have the wage.
Spent I-have the gold and all the silver,
well it you-see that I not carry [nothing],
sentences.i: If I live, I shall double your wages. The gold is spent and all the silver with it; you see well enough that I carry nothing,
sentences.n: doblar vos he = os doblaré, the split future again, two lines after querer m'a. soldada = the pay of a retained man (from sueldo). Espeso e = he gastado (espender, Latin expendere): aver is already doing modern haber's work as the perfect auxiliary. [nada] is Pidal's restoration — the Çid's literal claim to carry nothing is the one true statement the whole ruse will be built on.

sentences.t:
huebos me serié pora toda mi compaña;
fer lo he amidos, de grado non avrié nada.
sentences.l:
need to-me it-would-be for all my company;
to-do it I-will unwillingly, of good-will there-would-not-be nothing.
sentences.i: I should have need of it for my whole company; I shall do it against my will, for willingly there would be nothing to be had.
sentences.n: huebos (Latin opus) = 'need': huebos me serié, 'I should have need of it' — the word comes back in the lenders' own mouths at vv. 123 and 138. fer = fazer 'to do' in its short form, and fer lo he = lo haré, the split future a third time. amidos = 'unwillingly, under compulsion' (Latin invitus), repeated at v. 95: the Çid states twice over that the deception is forced on him.

sentences.i: With your counsel I mean to build two chests; let us fill them with sand, so that they will be good and heavy, covered in gilded leather and well studded with nails.
sentences.n: bastir, 'to build, rig up' — the verb that described Martín Antolínez's honest provisioning at v. 68 now describes a counterfeit. inchámoslas = hinchámoslas, 'let us fill them' (inchir, Latin implere). guadalmeçí is tooled and gilded leather of the costliest kind (the word is Arabic, from Ghadāmes); enclaveadas = 'studded with nails'. Everything about the outside of the chests is designed to be read as treasure — weight included.

sentences.t: Los guadameçís vermejos e los clavos bien dorados.
sentences.l: The gilded-leathers crimson and the nails well gilded.
sentences.i: The leathers crimson, and the nails bright with gilding.
sentences.n: Tirada 7 (assonance á-o) — the Çid sends Martín Antolínez to Raquel and Vidas to pawn the chests, and asks God to witness that he acts under compulsion. The tirada-break falls in the middle of the description of the chests: it is a change of assonance, not of subject, that makes a new tirada, and the sentence simply runs on across it. guadameçís is the same word as guadalmeçí one line earlier, now without the l — the edition keeps both spellings. vermejos = bermejos, 'bright red'.

sentences.t:
Por Raquel e Vidas vayádesme privado:
quando en Burgos me vedaron compra y el rey me a ayrado,
non puedo traer el aver, ca mucho es pesado,
sentences.l:
For Raquel and Vidas go-you-for-me quickly:
since in Burgos they-forbade-me buying and the king me has angered-against,
not I-can carry the wealth, for much it-is heavy,
sentences.i: Go quickly for me to Raquel and Vidas: since they have barred me from buying in Burgos, and the king has set his wrath on me, I cannot carry my wealth with me, for it is very heavy,
sentences.n: vayádesme = vayades + me, 'go for me' — the old second-person-plural in -ades/-edes is everywhere in this part (sodes, vedes, catedes). Raquel and Vidas are the Jewish moneylenders of Burgos; the poem names them without hostility and makes them shrewd, courteous men of business. me vedaron compra looks straight back to the royal ban of vv. 62–63. el aver = 'wealth, property', aver used as a noun beside aver the verb.

sentences.t:
enpeñar gelo he por lo que f[o]re guisado;
de noche lo lieven, que non lo vean cristianos.
sentences.l:
to-pledge it-to-them I-will for that which may-be fitting;
by night let-them-carry it, that not it may-see Christians.
sentences.i: I shall pledge it to them for whatever is reckoned fitting; let them carry it off by night, so that no Christian may see it.
sentences.n: enpeñar gelo he = se lo empeñaré: the split future once more, with gelo (ge + lo, 'it to them'), ge being the ancestor of the modern se of se lo. f[o]re = fuere, the future subjunctive of ser, ordinary and alive in this language. que non lo vean cristianos means 'that nobody at all may see it' — but here the darkness serves a second purpose the lenders are not told of.

sentences.t:
Véalo el Criador con todos los sos santos,
yo más non puedo e amidos lo fago.”
sentences.l:
May-see-it the Creator with all the his saints,
I more not I-can and unwillingly it I-do.”
sentences.i: Let the Creator see it, and all his saints with him: I can do no more, and I do it against my will.”
sentences.n: Véalo el Criador — the Çid calls God to witness the very deception he is arranging, and the poem shows no sign of finding this strange: necessity (huebos) is his defence. los sos santos, article plus possessive again, as in las sus bocas. amidos lo fago closes the speech with the word that opened the plan at v. 84.

sentences.t:
Martín Antolínez non lo detar[da]va
passó por Burgos, al castiello entrava,
por Raquel e Vidas apriessa demandava.
sentences.l:
Martín Antolínez not it was-delaying
he-passed through Burgos, into-the castle he-was-entering,
for Raquel and Vidas in-haste he-was-asking.
sentences.i: Martín Antolínez lost no time over it: he crossed Burgos, rode up into the castle, and asked in haste after Raquel and Vidas.
sentences.n: Tirada 8 (assonance á-a) — three lines of pure movement, carrying Martín Antolínez into Burgos to find the lenders. A tirada can be as short as this: the assonance turns to á-a for the space of three imperfects in -ava (detar[da]va, entrava, demandava), and that is all that holds it together. detar[da]va = detardava, 'was delaying' (cf. non lo detardan, v. 105). al castiello — the castle quarter above the town.

sentences.t:
Raquel e Vidas en uno estavan amos,
en cuenta de sus averes, de los que avien ganados.
sentences.l:
Raquel and Vidas in one were both,
in the counting of their wealth, of that which they-had gained.
sentences.i: Raquel and Vidas were together, the pair of them, at the reckoning of their wealth, all that they had gained.
sentences.n: Tirada 9 (assonance á-o) — the whole bargain: Martín Antolínez talks the lenders into six hundred marks on the pledge of the chests, the chests are carried off, and the money comes back to the camp before cockcrow. It is by far the longest tirada of this part, and the á-o assonance holds through all seventy-four of its lines (only se apartaron, v. 105, stands outside the pattern). The verse-numbering jumps straight from 98 to 100: no line 99 is printed anywhere in the edition, and the traditional count is left undisturbed. en uno = 'together, as one'; amos = ambos.

sentences.t:
Llegó Martín Antolínez a guisa de menbrado:
“¿O sodes, Raquel e Vidas, los mios amigos caros?
En poridad fablar querría con amos.”
sentences.l:
Arrived Martín Antolínez in the manner of a shrewd-man:
“Where are-you, Raquel and Vidas, the my dear friends?
In secret to-speak I-would-wish with both.”
sentences.i: Martín Antolínez came up like a man who knew what he was about: “Where are you, Raquel and Vidas, my dear friends? I should like to speak with you both in private.”
sentences.n: a guisa de menbrado = 'in the fashion of a prudent man' (menbrado, from membrar 'to bear in mind'); the formula is repeated word for word at v. 131, framing both his speeches. O = ó, 'where' (Latin ubi). poridad = 'secrecy, privacy' (from puridad 'purity'), so en poridad = 'in confidence'. los mios amigos — article plus possessive, as in las sus bocas.

sentences.t: Non lo detardan, todos tres se apartaron.
sentences.l: Not it they-delay, all three themselves drew-aside.
sentences.i: They do not delay: all three of them drew aside.
sentences.n: Non lo detardan takes up the verb of v. 96 and turns it to the present, and then the same sentence ends in the preterite (apartaron): the epic slides between tenses inside a single line. todos tres — the three-cornered withdrawal is the poridad he asked for. This is also the one line of the tirada whose ending (-áron) falls outside its á-o assonance.

sentences.i: “Raquel and Vidas, give me your hands on it, both of you: that you will not give me away to Moor or to Christian. I shall make you rich for all time, so that you may never be in want.
sentences.n: dar las manos — the handclasp that makes an agreement binding in Castilian custom; it will be stiffened into a sworn oath at v. 120 and recited as law at v. 163. descubrades = descubráis, 'reveal, betray'. a moros nin a cristianos = 'to a living soul', the standard merism (non … nin here is the ordinary correlative 'not … nor', ordinary in Spanish then and now, not the redundant double negative seen elsewhere). menguados, 'diminished, in want', returns as the Çid's own promise at v. 158.

sentences.t:
El Campeador por las parias f[o] entrado,
grandes averes priso e mucho sobejanos,
retovo dellos quanto que f[o] algo;
por en vino a aquesto por que f[o] acusado.
sentences.l:
The Campeador for the tributes had gone-in,
great wealth he-took and much exceeding,
he-kept-back of-it as-much as was something;
for this he-came to this (pass) for which he-was accused.
sentences.i: The Campeador had gone in to collect the tributes; great wealth he took, and vastly much of it, and he kept back from it whatever had value — that is how he came to this pass, and why he was accused.
sentences.n: parias — the tribute paid to Castile by the Muslim taifa kingdoms; collecting it was the historical Rodrigo Díaz's work in Andalusia, and the charge that he held part of it back is what the poem gives as the cause of the exile. f[o] = fue, the older preterite, restored three times in four lines. priso is the preterite of prender 'to take'; sobejanos = 'excessive, past measure'. Martín Antolínez's method is to stay with the truth as long as he can: all of this is common knowledge in Burgos.

sentences.t:
Tiene dos arcas llennas de oro esmerado.
Ya lo ve[e]des que el rey le a ayrado.
sentences.l:
He-has two chests full of gold refined.
Now it you-see that the king him has angered-against.
sentences.i: He has two chests full of refined gold. You see well enough that the king has set his wrath on him.
sentences.n: llennas = llenas. oro esmerado is assayed, purified gold, the costliest kind — the single outright lie of the speech, planted between two statements the lenders can check for themselves. le a ayrado: the king's ira is a legal condition, formal disgrace carrying banishment, not a mood; the Çid uses the same word of himself at v. 156.

sentences.t:
Dexado ha heredades e casas e palaçios.
Aquellas non las puede levar, sinon, serié ventad[o];
sentences.l:
Left he-has estates and houses and halls.
Those not them he-can carry-off, if-not, he-would-be scented-out;
sentences.i: He has left behind estates and houses and halls. The chests he cannot carry off with him, or he would be found out;
sentences.n: heredades = inherited landed property; palaçios here means great halls, not royal palaces. Aquellas, feminine plural, reaches back over casas and palaçios to the arcas of v. 113: it is the chests, not the estates, that cannot be moved openly. levar = llevar. ventado, from ventar 'to scent, to get wind of', is a hunting word — being nosed out is the fear on both sides of this bargain (again at v. 128, and as ventassen at v. 151).

sentences.t:
el Campeador dexar las ha en vuestra mano,
e prestalde de aver, lo que sea guisado.
sentences.l:
the Campeador to-leave them will in your hand,
and lend-to-him of wealth, that which may-be fitting.
sentences.i: The Campeador will leave them in your hands, and you are to lend him money, whatever is reasonable.
sentences.n: dexar las ha = las dejará, the split future with the pronoun tucked inside it. prestalde = prestadle, with the metathesis -dl- > -ld- that Old Spanish makes of imperative plus pronoun (so too Levaldas, v. 167). lo que sea guisado, 'whatever may be fitting' — the sum is left courteously unnamed for another seventeen lines, until the lenders themselves ask.

sentences.i: Take the chests and put them in your safe keeping; lay your sworn faith on it, both of you, with a great oath, that you will not look into them for a whole year.”
sentences.n: meted i las fe[de]s: i = 'therein' (Latin ibi, like French y), and fe[de]s is Pidal's restored older plural of fe 'pledged faith' (cf. fe[d], v. 163). catar here = 'to look into, inspect' — the same verb that meant 'to gaze' in v. 2. The year's grace is the whole ruse: the sand is to come to light only when the Çid is far out of reach.

sentences.t:
Raquel e Vidas seiense consejando:
“Nos huebos avemos en todo de ganar algo.
Bien lo sabemos que él algo [a] gañ[ado],
sentences.l:
Raquel and Vidas were-sitting themselves taking-counsel:
“We need have in everything to gain something.
Well it we-know that he something has gained,
sentences.i: Raquel and Vidas sat conferring together: “In all this we must get something for ourselves. We know well enough that he has come by something,
sentences.n: seiense consejando: seer (Latin sedere) still carries both 'to sit' and 'to be', so this is 'they sat taking counsel' — the lenders withdraw to confer, just as Martín Antolínez drew all three aside at v. 105. huebos avemos, 'we have need': the Çid's word for his necessity (v. 83) is also their word for their profit. algo, 'something', is this poem's discreet term for money (vv. 111, 157). [a] gañ[ado] is Pidal's restoration of the perfect.

sentences.t:
quando a tierra de moros entró, que grant aver [a] sac[ado];
non duerme sin sospecha qui aver trae monedado.
sentences.l:
when to land of Moors he-entered, that great wealth he-has taken-out;
not he-sleeps without suspicion who wealth carries coined.
sentences.i: for when he went into the land of the Moors, he brought great wealth out of it; and no man who travels with coined money sleeps free of fear.
sentences.n: The pair reason their way toward the truth from the outside: they never ask what is in the chests, only what a man back from the parias is likely to hold, and why he would want it off his hands overnight. qui = 'he who' (Latin qui), the old relative. aver monedado is wealth in struck coin as against land or stock — the kind that can be carried off, hence the sleeplessness.

sentences.t:
Estas arcas, prendámoslas am[o]s,
en logar las metamos que non sea ventad[o].
sentences.l:
These chests, let-us-take-them both,
in a-place let-us-put-them that not it-may-be scented-out.
sentences.i: These chests — let us take them, the two of us, and put them somewhere it will not be nosed out.
sentences.n: prendámoslas, metamos: hortative subjunctives (first-person-plural 'let's…'), the decision taken openly between them. am[o]s is Pidal's restoration of the form that runs right through the tirada (amos, vv. 100, 104, 106, 120, 173). ventado for the second time in a dozen lines: the lenders' caution matches the Çid's word for word, which is exactly why the bargain can be struck.

sentences.t:
Mas dezidnos del Çid, de qué será pagado,
o qué ganançia nos dará por todo aqueste año?”
sentences.l:
But tell-us of the Çid, with what will-he-be satisfied,
or what gain to-us will-he-give for all this year?”
sentences.i: But tell us about the Çid: what will content him, and what profit will he give us for this whole year?”
sentences.n: será pagado — pagarse again, in the sense 'to be satisfied', which shades straight into 'to be paid' (cf. Pagós, v. 69; me pago, v. 141; nos pagamos, v. 146). ganançia is the interest on the loan, asked for plainly and treated as a matter of course: the poem reports the transaction without moralizing over either party.

sentences.i: Martín Antolínez answered like a shrewd man: “My Çid will want only what is reasonable; he will ask little of you for leaving his wealth in safe keeping.
sentences.n: Respuso = respondió, the strong preterite of responder. a guisa de menbrado repeats v. 102 exactly — the narrator's own verdict on the performance. aguisado is the same word as guisado (v. 118), 'fitting, reasonable': the courteous screen over a hard piece of haggling. pedir vos a = os pedirá, yet another split future.

sentences.t:
Acógensele omnes de todas partes me[n]guados,
a menester seysçientos marcos.”
sentences.l:
There-gather-to-him men from all parts needy,
he-has need six-hundred marks.”
sentences.i: Needy men are gathering to him from every quarter; he has need of six hundred marks.”
sentences.n: Acógensele = acógense + le, 'they take themselves in to him', with reflexive and dative both glued to the verb. me[n]guados, the word used of the lenders' own future at v. 108, here means the poor who flock to the exile: the loan is to feed an army. seysçientos marcos is silver by weight, the figure that governs the rest of the tirada. v. 135 is conspicuously short for this verse and may be defective in the copy; Pidal prints it as it stands.

sentences.t: Dixo Raquel e Vidas: “dar gelos [hemos] de grado.”
sentences.l: Said Raquel and Vidas: “to-give them-to-him we-will gladly.”
sentences.i: Raquel and Vidas said: “We will gladly give them to him.”
sentences.n: Dixo with two names as its subject: Raquel and Vidas speak throughout under one singular verb, as a single trading house. dar gelos [hemos] = se los daremos — the split future with [hemos] restored by Pidal; gelos = ge + los, 'them to him'. de grado answers the Çid's own de grado non avrié nada at v. 84.

sentences.t:
—“Ya vedes que entra la noch, el Çid es pressurado,
huebos avemos que nos dedes los marcos.”
sentences.l:
—“Now you-see that enters the night, the Çid is pressed,
need we-have that to-us you-give the marks.”
sentences.i: —“You see that night is coming in, and the Çid is pressed for time; we have need that you hand over the marks.”
sentences.n: The dash is Pidal's: it is Martín Antolínez speaking again, without being named — que nos dedes shows he is pressing Raquel e Vidas, not the reverse — and the bargaining runs on as bare exchange. noch = noche, apocopated (cf. anoch, v. 42). pressurado = apresurado, 'hurried, under pressure'. huebos avemos for the third time in this part (vv. 83, 123) — every party to this bargain pleads necessity.

sentences.t:
Dixo Raquel e Vidas: “non se faze assí el mercado,
sinon primero prendiendo e después dando.”
sentences.l:
Said Raquel and Vidas: “not itself is-done thus the bargain,
but-rather first taking and afterwards giving.”
sentences.i: Raquel and Vidas said: “That is not how a bargain is done — first the taking, and afterwards the giving.”
sentences.n: el mercado here is the transaction, the deal, not a market-place. The maxim is put in bare gerunds, prendiendo … dando, with no finite verb at all: goods in hand first, money after. It is the one point at which the lenders set the terms, courteously and immovably.

sentences.t: Dixo Martín Antolínez: “yo desso me pago.
sentences.l: Said Martín Antolínez: “I with-that myself content.
sentences.i: Martín Antolínez said: “I am content with that.
sentences.n: desso = de esso. me pago = 'I am satisfied with it' — the third turn of pagarse in a dozen lines (vv. 129, 136, 146): it is the verb by which this negotiation records each of its agreements.

sentences.t:
Amos tred al Campeador contado,
e nos vos ayudaremos, que assí es aguisado,
por aducir las arcas e meterlas en vuestro salvo,
que non lo sepan moros nin cristianos.”
sentences.l:
Both come to the Campeador renowned,
and we you will-help, for thus it-is fitting,
to bring the chests and to-put-them in your safe-keeping,
that not it may-know Moors nor Christians.”
sentences.i: Come, both of you, to the renowned Campeador, and we shall help you, as is only right, to bring the chests away and put them in your safe keeping, so that neither Moor nor Christian may know of it.”
sentences.n: tred is the imperative of trer/traer in its old intransitive sense 'come along' (Latin trahere). contado = 'reckoned up, renowned', a standing epithet of the Campeador in this tirada (again at v. 152). aducir = 'to bring, fetch' (Latin adducere; past participle aduchas, v. 147). The secrecy clause repeats the Çid's own at v. 93 almost word for word: both sides want the same darkness, for different reasons.

sentences.t:
Dixo Raquel e Vidas: “nos desto nos pagamos.
Las archas aduchas, prendet seyesçientos marcos.”
sentences.l:
Said Raquel and Vidas: “we with-this ourselves content.
The chests brought, take six-hundred marks.”
sentences.i: Raquel and Vidas said: “We are content with that. Once the chests are brought, take your six hundred marks.”
sentences.n: archas here, arcas two lines above, and seyesçientos here against seysçientos at v. 135: the copyist's spelling wavers and the edition keeps each form as written (so too guadalmeçí/guadameçís). Las archas aduchas is an absolute phrase of the Latin kind, 'the chests once brought', like la oraçión fecha at v. 54; aduchas is the past participle of aducir.

sentences.t:
Martín Antolínez caualgó privado
con Raquel e Vidas, de voluntad e de grado.
sentences.l:
Martín Antolínez rode quickly
with Raquel and Vidas, of will and of pleasure.
sentences.i: Martín Antolínez rode off smartly with Raquel and Vidas, willingly and with a good grace.
sentences.n: caualgó keeps the copyist's u for v, as printed (cf. llegaua, dava in the opening tiradas). privado as an adverb = 'quickly, promptly' (so too vv. 89 and 166). de voluntad e de grado is a doubled formula whose two halves say the same thing — the regular way of filling out a hemistich in this verse.

sentences.t:
Non viene a la puent, ca por el agua a passado,
que gelo non ventassen de Burgos omne nado.
sentences.l:
Not he-comes to the bridge, for through the water he-has crossed,
that it-to-him not should-scent-out of Burgos man born.
sentences.i: He does not come by the bridge: he has crossed through the water, so that no man born in Burgos should get wind of it.
sentences.n: The bridge over the Arlanzón is the open, overlooked way into the town; the ford is not. omne nado, 'man born', is the same all-inclusive idiom as moros nin cristianos. ventassen is the hunting word for the third time (vv. 116, 128), the scent now literally on the night air. Tense-mixing again: viene in the present beside a passado and the imperfect subjunctive ventassen.

sentences.t:
Afévoslos a la tienda del Campeador contado;
assí commo entraron, al Çid besáronle las manos.
sentences.l:
Behold-you-them at the tent of-the Campeador renowned;
as soon-as they-entered, to-the Çid they-kissed-him the hands.
sentences.i: And there they are at the tent of the renowned Campeador; as soon as they entered, they kissed the Çid's hands.
sentences.n: Afévoslos = afé + vos + los, 'here they are for you': afé is the poem's pointing word, whose origin is disputed (Arabic hā 'behold' has been proposed), and here it carries two pronouns at once — the boldest enclitic squeeze of this part. besar las manos is the formal courtesy owed to a lord, performed here by the men who are about to become his creditors.

sentences.t:
Sonrrisós mio Çid, estávalos fablando:
“¡ya don Raquel e Vidas, avédesme olbidado!
Ya me exco de tierra, ca del rey so ayrado.
sentences.l:
Smiled-himself my Çid, was-them speaking-to:
“O don Raquel and Vidas, you-have-me forgotten!
Now myself I-go-out from land, for by-the king I-am angered-against.
sentences.i: My Çid smiled, and stood speaking with them: “Ah, don Raquel and Vidas, you have quite forgotten me! Now I am going out of the land, for the king's wrath is upon me.
sentences.n: Sonrrisós = sonrrisóse, the -se worn down to -s after the stressed vowel (cf. tornós, Partiós in the opening tiradas). estávalos fablando = 'was speaking to them', the pronoun glued inside the periphrasis. The smile is the poem's only comment on the trick, and avédesme olbidado is a host's mock-reproach from the man doing the deceiving. exco = salgo, the old first person of exir (Latin exire; cf. exien, v. 16). so ayrado = 'I am in the king's ira', the formula of v. 114 now in his own mouth.

sentences.t:
A lo quem semeja, de lo mio avredes algo;
mientra que vivades non seredes menguados.”
sentences.l:
By that-which to-me seems, of the mine you-will-have something;
while that you-may-live not you-will-be in-want.”
sentences.i: As it seems to me, you shall have something of what is mine; as long as you live you shall not be in want.”
sentences.n: quem = que me, the pronoun worn down to a single consonant (cf. nol, and assil at v. 163). de lo mio avredes algo — algo once more as 'a share of wealth' (vv. 111, 123). The sentence repeats Martín Antolínez's promise at v. 108 almost word for word (non seades / non seredes menguados): the two men of the trick say the same thing twice over, which is how this verse builds its refrains.

sentences.t: Raquel e Vidas a mio Çid besáronle las manos.
sentences.l: Raquel and Vidas to my Çid they-kissed-him the hands.
sentences.i: Raquel and Vidas kissed my Çid's hands.
sentences.n: The line repeats v. 153 almost exactly and closes the audience as it opened — the gesture frames the scene. a mio Çid … besáronle: the person is marked twice, once by the preposition and once by the enclitic le, which is ordinary here and not emphatic.

sentences.i: Martín Antolínez has settled the agreement: that on the security of those chests they would give him six hundred marks, and would guard them well until the year was out;
sentences.n: pleyto (Latin placitum) = a covenant, terms agreed; parar el pleyto = 'to settle the terms'. dar le ien = le darían, the split conditional with the pronoun tucked inside, the same construction as conbidar le ien in the opening tiradas. gelas = ge las, 'them for him'. From here the narrator recites the contract as a charter would: sum, security, term, and then the penalty.

sentences.t:
ca assil dieran la fe[d] e gelo auien jurado,
que si antes las catassen que f[o]ssen perjurados,
non les diesse mio Çid de ganançia un dinero malo.
sentences.i: for they had given him their pledged faith on it and sworn it to him: that if they looked into the chests before the term, they would be forsworn, and my Çid need give them not one bad penny of profit.
sentences.n: assil = assí + l(e), 'thus to him'. fe[d] is Pidal's restored older form of fe (cf. fe[de]s, v. 120), the sworn faith that makes the clause binding. auien keeps the copyist's u for v. un dinero malo, 'one bad penny', is a debased coin, the smallest thing worth naming — contempt measured in small change, as with un figo at v. 77. The penalty is forfeiture of the whole ganançia, drafted exactly as a real charter would draft it.

sentences.t:
Dixo Martín Antolínez: “carguen las arcas privado.
Levaldas, Raquel e Vidas, ponedlas en vuestro salvo;
yo iré convus[c]o, que adugamos los marcos,
ca a mover [h]a mio Çid ante que cante el gallo.”
sentences.l:
Said Martín Antolínez: “let-them-load the chests quickly.
Carry-them, Raquel and Vidas, put-them in your safe-keeping;
I will-go with-you, that we-may-bring the marks,
for to move has my Çid before that may-sing the cock.”
sentences.i: Martín Antolínez said: “Load up the chests, and quickly. Carry them off, Raquel and Vidas, and put them in your safe keeping; I will go with you, so that we may bring back the marks — for my Çid must be on the move before the cock crows.”
sentences.n: Levaldas = llevadlas, with the metathesis of imperative plus pronoun (cf. prestalde, v. 118). convus[c]o = con + vusco, 'with you', the fused form already seen as con vusco at v. 75. a mover [h]a = ha de mover, 'he has to set out': aver a + infinitive for obligation, the ancestor of modern haber de. ante que cante el gallo fixes the deadline — the whole business has to close in the dark.

sentences.t:
Al cargar de las arcas veriedes gozo tanto:
Non las podien poner en somo maguer eran esforçados.
sentences.l:
At-the loading of the chests you-would-have-seen joy so-great:
Not them they-could put on-top although they-were strong.
sentences.i: At the loading of the chests you would have seen such delight: they could not heave them up on top, strong men though they were.
sentences.n: veriedes = veríais, 'you would have seen' — the minstrel turning to his audience, as with odredes at v. 70. en somo = 'on top' (of the pack-beasts). maguer = 'although', a rare word in Spanish and Greek in origin. The joke lies in the weight: the sand is doing its work, and the lenders' delight is in the very heaviness that proves the fraud.

sentences.t:
Grádanse Raquel e Vidas con averes monedados,
ca mientra que visquiessen refechos eran amos.
sentences.l:
Rejoice-themselves Raquel and Vidas with wealth coined,
for while that they-might-live made-rich were both.
sentences.i: Raquel and Vidas rejoice over wealth in coin, for as long as they should live the two of them were made men.
sentences.n: Grádanse (gradarse, 'to take pleasure') holds the present, and then eran swings back into the past inside the same sentence. refechos (past participle of refazer) = 'restored, set up again, made rich'. averes monedados closes the tirada on the phrase the lenders used in their own reasoning at v. 126; whether it means the coin they have just handed over or the gold they believe they hold in pledge is genuinely open, and the poem ends the tirada without saying what is in the chests.
